text:
ANNALS OF THE DAY  🪔

A Historical Chronicle of October 2

“We carry yesterday like a lantern—not to light the road behind us, but to see how far we’ve already come, and how much farther we need to go.” ~ Hodgepodgery

October 2 has witnessed pivotal historical and political moments, scientific breakthroughs, cultural shifts, notable births and deaths, and sports milestones.

Calendar Overview  🧭

October 2 is the 275th day of the year (≈75.34% through the year) in the Gregorian calendar, assuming a non-leap year such as 2026. There are 90 days (≈24.66%) remaining in the year after October 2, through December 31. It falls in the 40th week of the year under ISO week numbering. October 2 is also associated with various holidays and observances, including the International Day of Non-Violence and National Name Your Car Day.

Calendar Overview acts as structured date context—turning a simple date into useful information about progress, scheduling position, and relevant observances.

Historical and Political Events  🏛️

October 2 has been the date of major changes in kingdoms, revolutions, wars, independence movements, governments, and international affairs.

🥈1187 — Saladin Captures Jerusalem.  ⚔️

After a short siege, the Crusader garrison of Jerusalem surrendered to Saladin, ending Frankish rule of the city that had begun with the First Crusade in 1099.

 🧩 TRIVIA: Unlike the 1099 conquest, Saladin allowed most Christian residents to leave after paying a ransom rather than ordering a general massacre.

1263 — Battle of Largs.  ⚔️

Norwegian forces under King Haakon IV clashed with the Scots on the Firth of Clyde in a storm-disrupted fight that checked the last major Viking campaign in western Scotland. 

🧩 TRIVIA: The inconclusive battle still led to the 1266 Treaty of Perth, in which Norway ceded the Hebrides and the Isle of Man to Scotland.

1470 — Edward IV Driven from England.

The Earl of Warwick’s rebellion forced King Edward IV to flee to the Burgundian Netherlands and briefly restored the deposed Henry VI in what is called the Readeption.

🧩 TRIVIA: The restoration lasted only months; Edward returned in 1471, defeated Warwick at Barnet, and retook the throne.

1535 — Cartier Reaches Hochelaga.

On his second voyage to the Gulf of St. Lawrence, French explorer Jacques Cartier reached Hochelaga, a St. Lawrence Iroquoian town on the site of present-day Montreal.

🧩 TRIVIA: Cartier climbed the hill he named Mont Réal, the origin of Montreal’s name.

1552 — Fall of Kazan.  ⚔️

Ivan IV’s Russian army took the Khanate of Kazan after a long siege, the first major conquest in the expansion of Muscovy down the Volga. 

🧩 TRIVIA: The victory is commemorated by St. Basil’s Cathedral in Moscow, begun the same year.

🥇1789 — Bill of Rights Sent to the States.  📜

President George Washington transmitted the constitutional amendments proposed by the First Congress to the state legislatures for ratification. 

🧩 TRIVIA: Congress had approved twelve amendments; only ten were ratified in 1791, and one of the rejected pair later became the Twenty-seventh Amendment in 1992.

1835 — Battle of Gonzales.  ⚔️

Mexican troops sent to reclaim a small cannon from the settlement of Gonzales were turned back by Texian militia, the first fight of the Texas Revolution. 

🧩 TRIVIA: The settlers’ flag carried the slogan “Come and Take It” above a picture of the cannon.

1935 — Italy Invades Ethiopia.  ⚔️

After Italian forces crossed the frontier, Emperor Haile Selassie ordered a general mobilization, opening the Second Italo-Ethiopian War.

🧩 TRIVIA: The League of Nations condemned the invasion but its sanctions left oil and other key supplies largely untouched.

1941 — Operation Typhoon Begins.  ⚔️

Germany launched its main autumn offensive toward Moscow, with Army Group Center (Heeresgruppe Mitte) driving on the Soviet capital before winter. 

🧩 TRIVIA: The attack opened with huge encirclements at Vyazma and Bryansk, but mud, then frost, and Soviet reinforcements stopped the drive short of the city.

1944 — Warsaw Uprising Ends. 

Surviving fighters of the Polish Home Army capitulated to German forces after 63 days, ending the uprising that had begun as the Red Army neared the city. 

🧩 TRIVIA: The surrender terms treated the Home Army as combatants rather than partisans, allowing many fighters to go into German POW camps instead of being shot.

1967 — Thurgood Marshall Joins the Supreme Court.  ⚖️

Thurgood Marshall was sworn in as an associate justice, the first African American member of the United States Supreme Court. 

🧩 TRIVIA: Before the bench he had argued Brown v. Board of Education and won 29 of the 32 cases he took to the Court for the NAACP.

1968 — Tlatelolco Massacre.  ✊

Mexican security forces fired on student demonstrators gathered in the Plaza de las Tres Culturas in Mexico City, ten days before the opening of the Olympic Games. 

🧩 TRIVIA: The government long put the death toll in the dozens; later investigations and witness accounts have placed it in the hundreds.

1986 — Senate Overrides Apartheid Veto. The U.S. Senate overrode President Ronald Reagan’s veto of the Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act, imposing sanctions on South Africa. 

🧩 TRIVIA: It was the first foreign-policy veto override of Reagan’s presidency and passed with support from both parties.

Scientific, Technological, and Cultural Milestones  🚀

Scientific firsts, engineering achievements, and cultural turning points.

1608 — Lippershey’s telescope reaches the record.  🔭

On October 2, 1608, the States General of the Netherlands considered spectacle-maker Hans Lippershey’s patent request for a tube with a convex lens and a concave eyepiece that magnified about three times—the earliest surviving written record of a working telescope.

🧩 TRIVIA: The patent was refused because the idea could not be kept secret; within months Jacob Metius filed a rival claim, and a year later simple telescopes were already circulating across Europe.

🥉1836 — Darwin comes home from the Beagle.  🚢

On October 2, 1836, Charles Darwin landed back in England after nearly five years aboard HMS Beagle, carrying the notes, fossils, and specimens that later underpinned his argument for evolution by natural selection. 

🧩 TRIVIA: The voyage was planned for two years; Darwin, nearly barred for lacking formal natural-history credentials, used the extra time to catalogue Galápagos finches and South American fossils.

1925 — Baird sends the first grayscale television picture.  📺

On October 2, 1925, in a Soho laboratory, John Logie Baird transmitted a moving image with tone, not just silhouette: the head of a ventriloquist’s dummy, scanned in 30 lines at about five pictures a second. He then pulled in office clerk William Taynton, who became the first person televised in full tonal range. 

🧩 TRIVIA: The dummy was nicknamed Stooky Bill, and Taynton was paid half a crown after the hot lights drove him out of the chair; a newspaper editor later dismissed Baird as a possibly dangerous lunatic claiming he could “see by wireless.”

🎁 EXTRA BONUS:  After successfully transmitting the image of a ventriloquist's dummy named Stooky Bill, Baird needed to test a real human face. He ran downstairs and bribed a 20-year-old office clerk named William Taynton with 2 shillings and 6 pence (half a crown) to sit in front of his apparatus.

When Baird stepped back into the receiver room, the screen went completely dark. Confused, he walked back to the transmitter and found that Taynton was so frightened by the blinding light bulbs and high-voltage equipment that he had backed away from the camera lens!

Baird had to pay Taynton an extra half-crown bonus to persuade him to stay under the scorching heat lamps, finally making Taynton the first human face ever televised in full tonal range.

1950 — Peanuts begins.

On October 2, 1950, Charles M. Schulz’s comic strip Peanuts (adapted from his earlier panel Li’l Folks) debuted in seven U.S. newspapers, introducing Charlie Brown, Shermy, and Patty.

 🧩 TRIVIA: Schulz had nearly called Charlie Brown’s dog Sniffy, then found another comic already used that name; Snoopy himself did not appear until the strip of October 4.

1959 — The Twilight Zone premieres.  🌀

On October 2, 1959, Rod Serling’s anthology series opened on CBS with “Where Is Everybody?,” about a man alone in an empty town. The reveal is that he is an Air Force trainee cracking after 484 hours in an isolation chamber meant to simulate a trip to the Moon. 

🧩 TRIVIA: Serling wrote the episode and spoke the narration himself; a 1958 Time article on real isolation experiments, and a trainee named Don Farrell, helped shape the story of Mike Ferris.

1965 — Gatorade is tried in a real game.

 On October 2, 1965, University of Florida players drank a lab-made salt-and-sugar solution on the sideline against LSU in about 102-degree heat. Dr. Robert Cade and colleagues had mixed it to replace fluid and electrolytes lost in sweat; Florida won as the favored Tigers wilted.

 🧩 TRIVIA: Early batches tasted so bad that some athletes vomited; Cade’s wife suggested lemon juice, and the drink had already been tried the day before in a freshman-versus-varsity scrimmage.

2023 — The mRNA Nobel is announced.  🧬

On October 2, 2023, the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman for nucleoside base modifications that let messenger RNA be used in medicine without triggering a destructive immune response, the work behind the COVID-19 mRNA vaccines. 

🧩 TRIVIA: Their key papers were repeatedly rejected before publication; Karikó had been demoted at the University of Pennsylvania years earlier for insisting on mRNA research.

Famous Birthdays  🎂

Here are notable October 2nd birthdays throughout history, featuring famous historical figures, scientists, writers, actors, and musicians.

1452 — Richard III "Crouchback", the last Plantagenet king of England, who took the crown in 1483 and died at the Battle of Bosworth Field. 

🧩 TRIVIA: His skeleton was found under a Leicester car park in 2012 and reburied in the city’s cathedral in 2015. Born in Fotheringhay, Northamptonshire.

1800 — Nat Turner, an enslaved preacher who led the 1831 Southampton rebellion, the largest slave uprising in U.S. history. 

🧩 TRIVIA: He hid for about two months before capture and was hanged on November 11, 1831. Born in Southampton County, Virginia.

1847 — Paul von Hindenburg, the German field marshal and later Weimar president who appointed Hitler chancellor in 1933. 

🧩 TRIVIA: With Ludendorff he was credited with the 1914 victory at Tannenberg. Born in Posen, Prussia (now Poznań, Poland).

1869 — Mahatma Gandhi, the Indian lawyer and independence leader who built a mass movement around nonviolent resistance. 

🧩 TRIVIA: India marks his birthday as Gandhi Jayanti, a national holiday. Born in Porbandar, India.

1890 — Julius Henry "Groucho" Marx, the American comedian and Marx Brother known for the painted mustache, cigar, and rapid insult. 

🧩 TRIVIA: He hosted the quiz show You Bet Your Life from 1947 to 1961. Born in New York City.

1904 — Henry Graham Greene, the English novelist of The Power and the Glory, The Quiet American, and Our Man in Havana. 

🧩 TRIVIA: He divided his own books into “entertainments” and serious novels. Born in Berkhamsted, Hertfordshire.

1928 — George “Spanky” McFarland, the American child actor who led the Our Gang comedies in the 1930s. 

🧩 TRIVIA: He was hired after a studio talent search for a round-faced boy and stayed with the series into his teens. Born in Dallas, Texas.

1938 — Rex Reed (age 88), the American film critic and columnist long associated with the New York Observer. 🧩 TRIVIA: He acted opposite Mae West in the 1970 film Myra Breckinridge. Born in Fort Worth, Texas.

1945 — Don McLean "American Troubadour" (age 81), the American singer-songwriter of “American Pie” and “Vincent.” 

🧩 TRIVIA: “American Pie” runs more than eight minutes and was cut for radio before the full version became a hit. Born in New Rochelle, New York.

1948 — Avery Brooks (age 78), the American actor who played Captain Benjamin Sisko on Star Trek: Deep Space Nine. 

🧩 TRIVIA: He was also Hawk on Spenser: For Hire and a trained opera singer. Born in Evansville, Indiana.

1948 — Donna Karan "The Queen of Seventh Avenue" (age 78), the American designer who built DKNY and made the simple black bodysuit a signature. 

🧩 TRIVIA: She worked for Anne Klein before launching her own label in 1984. Born in New York City.

1949 — Annie Leibovitz (age 77), the American photographer known for Rolling Stone and Vanity Fair portraits. 

🧩 TRIVIA: Her 1980 photo of John Lennon and Yoko Ono was taken hours before Lennon was killed. Born in Waterbury, Connecticut.

1950 — Mike Rutherford "The Dumbledore of rock" (age 76), the English guitarist and bassist of Genesis and Mike + the Mechanics. 

🧩 TRIVIA: With Phil Collins and Tony Banks he is one of the three members who stayed with Genesis from the late 1960s into the 1990s. Born in Guildford, Surrey.

1951 — Sting (born Gordon Sumner; age 75), the English singer, frontman of The Police, and a solo star.

🧩 TRIVIA: A teacher nicknamed him Sting because of a black-and-yellow striped sweater that looked like a bee. Born in Wallsend, England.

1954 — Lorraine Bracco (age 72), the American actress who played Karen Hill in Goodfellas and Dr. Jennifer Melfi on The Sopranos. 

🧩 TRIVIA: She received an Academy Award nomination for Goodfellas. Born in Brooklyn, New York.

1970 — Kelly Ripa (age 56), the American actress and host of the syndicated morning show Live with Kelly and Mark. 

🧩 TRIVIA: She spent more than a decade as Hayley Vaughan on All My Children before joining Regis Philbin in 2001. Born in Stratford, New Jersey.

In Memoriam  🥀

Here are notable deaths of historical figures, scientists, writers, actors, entertainers, and musicians that occurred on October 2 throughout history.

534 AD — Athalaric (aged 18), King of the Ostrogoths in Italy who inherited the throne as a child under his mother Amalasuntha’s regency, died of illness after a short and troubled reign. 

🧩 TRIVIA: Contemporary accounts blamed his decline on a lifestyle of heavy drinking encouraged by Gothic nobles who resented Roman-style schooling.

829 — Michael II "the Stammerer" (aged about 59), Byzantine emperor nicknamed “the Amorian” or “the Stammerer,” founder of the Amorian dynasty, died of kidney disease. 

🧩 TRIVIA: He rose from an ordinary soldier to emperor after helping assassinate Leo V in 820.

939 — Gilbert, Duke of Lorraine (aged about 49), Frankish noble who rebelled against Otto I, drowned while trying to escape across the Rhine after the Battle of Andernach. 

🧩 TRIVIA: His death helped Otto I consolidate power in the early Holy Roman Empire.

1264 — Pope Urban IV, born James Pantaleon, (aged about 64), French pope who had been patriarch of Jerusalem, died of illness at Perugia. 

🧩 TRIVIA: He offered the crown of Sicily to Charles of Anjou, a move that pulled the papacy deeper into Italian power struggles.

1780 — John André (aged 29), British Army major and spymaster who negotiated Benedict Arnold’s planned surrender of West Point, was hanged as a spy by the Continental Army. 

🧩 TRIVIA: He had been captured with Arnold’s papers hidden in his boot after missing a rendezvous with the British ship HMS Vulture.

1803 — Samuel Adams (aged 81), American revolutionary leader, signer of the Declaration of Independence, and governor of Massachusetts, died of natural causes in Boston. 

🧩 TRIVIA: He organized the Boston Tea Party network and was once called the “Father of the American Revolution.”

1853 — François Arago (aged 67), French physicist, astronomer, and briefly prime minister, died of complications from diabetes. 

🧩 TRIVIA: He helped prove the wave theory of light and sponsored the work that led to the discovery of Neptune.

1920 — Max Bruch (aged 82), German Romantic composer best known for his Violin Concerto No. 1 and Kol Nidrei, died in Berlin. 

🧩 TRIVIA: He disliked being remembered only for the violin concerto and considered other works more important.

1927 — Svante Arrhenius (aged 68), Swedish chemist and physicist who won the 1903 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the theory of electrolytic dissociation, died of acute intestinal illness. 

🧩 TRIVIA: He was among the first scientists to calculate how carbon dioxide could warm the Earth’s climate.

1968 — Marcel Duchamp "Rrose Sélavy" (aged 81), French-American artist who helped launch Dada and conceptual art with works such as Nude Descending a Staircase and the readymade Fountain, died in his sleep in Neuilly-sur-Seine. 

🧩 TRIVIA: For decades he claimed to have given up art, while secretly building the installation Étant donnés.

1973 — Paavo Nurmi (aged 76), Finnish distance runner who won nine Olympic gold medals, died of atherosclerosis in Helsinki. 

🧩 TRIVIA: Known as the “Flying Finn,” he often raced with a stopwatch in his hand to pace himself.

1985 — Rock Hudson (born Roy Harold Scherer Jr.; aged 59), American actor famous for Pillow Talk, Giant, and Ice Station Zebra, died of AIDS-related complications in Beverly Hills. 

🧩 TRIVIA: He was one of the first major Hollywood stars whose death made AIDS a widely discussed public issue.

1987 — Peter Medawar, “the father of transplantation” (aged 72), the Brazilian-born British biologist who shared the 1960 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his work on immune tolerance, died in London after a stroke.

🧩 TRIVIA: His research on graft rejection helped make organ transplantation possible.

1998 — Gene Autry (aged 91), American singing cowboy, actor, and songwriter of “Back in the Saddle Again,” died of lymphoma in Studio City, California. 

🧩 TRIVIA: He owned the Los Angeles Angels baseball team from 1961 to 1997 and is the only person with stars in all five Hollywood Walk of Fame categories.

2005 — August Wilson,"the theater's poet of Black America" (aged 60), American playwright of the Pittsburgh Cycle, including Fences and The Piano Lesson, died of liver cancer in Seattle. 

🧩 TRIVIA: He won two Pulitzer Prizes for drama and wrote ten plays covering each decade of the twentieth-century African American experience.

2016 — Neville Marriner, "one of the world's greatest conductors" (aged 92), British conductor who founded the Academy of St Martin in the Fields, died in London. 

🧩 TRIVIA: His orchestra’s recording of the score for Amadeus became one of the best-selling classical albums ever.

2017 — Tom Petty, (aged 66), American rock singer and songwriter with Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers and the Traveling Wilburys, died of an accidental drug overdose in Santa Monica. 

🧩 TRIVIA: He wrote “Free Fallin’” as a quick sketch about the San Fernando Valley and finished the song in one session.

2018 — Jamal Khashoggi (aged 59), Saudi journalist and Washington Post columnist, was assassinated inside the Saudi consulate in Istanbul. 

🧩 TRIVIA: He had gone to the consulate to collect papers needed for his marriage.

2020 — Bob Gibson, "Gibby" (aged 84), St. Louis Cardinals pitcher and Baseball Hall of Famer, died of pancreatic cancer in Omaha. 

🧩 TRIVIA: In 1968 he posted a 1.12 ERA, the lowest in modern major-league history, and won both the Cy Young Award and MVP.

2022 — Sacheen Littlefeather (born Marie Louise Cruz; aged 75), an American actress and activist who declined the Academy Award on behalf of Marlon Brando at the 1973 Oscars, died of breast cancer in Novato, California.

🧩 TRIVIA: Brando asked her to speak against Hollywood’s portrayal of Native Americans during the Godfather win.

Sports Highlights  ⚾️

Here's Sports Highlights for October 2nd.

1876 — Bob Martin, “The St Andrews Wizard,” won the Open Championship at St Andrews after he and Davie Strath tied at 176 and Strath refused to play off.

🧩 TRIVIA: Martin, a St Andrews caddie who worked for Old Tom Morris, walked the course alone on Monday and was declared champion.

1908 — Addie Joss, "the Human Hairpin" of the Cleveland Naps throws a perfect game against the Chicago White Sox, winning 1–0 at League Park. 

🧩 TRIVIA: Joss needed only 74 pitches, the fewest known in a perfect game, and outdueled Ed Walsh, who struck out 15 and finished the day at 39–15.

1914 — Boston Red Sox rookie Babe Ruth doubles for his first major-league hit and earns his second pitching win in an 11–5 victory over the New York Yankees. 

🧩 TRIVIA: Ruth’s first hit came in the same season he made his debut as a pitcher, years before he became the game’s most famous slugger.

1920 — The Cincinnati Reds and Pittsburgh Pirates play the last tripleheader in major-league history at Forbes Field. 

🧩 TRIVIA: The Reds won the first two games, 13–4 and 7–3, and the Pirates took the six-inning nightcap, 6–0.

1921 — Babe Ruth hits his 59th home run of the season for the New York Yankees, stretching the single-season record he already held. 

🧩 TRIVIA: The homer came on the final day of the season off Boston’s Curt Fullerton in a 7–6 Yankees win.

1932 — The New York Yankees complete a four-game World Series sweep of the Chicago Cubs, 13–6, and extend their Fall Classic winning streak to 12 games. 

🧩 TRIVIA: The same day, the NFL’s Boston Braves — the franchise that later became the Washington Commanders — played their first league game and lost 14–0 to the Brooklyn Dodgers.

1938 — Cleveland’s Bob Feller, “Rapid Robert,” struck out 18 Detroit Tigers, a major-league single-game record at the time, but the Indians still lost 4–1.

🧩 TRIVIA: Feller was 19 years old and set the mark in a game his team did not win.

1947 — Yogi Berra, "Yogi" hits the first pinch-hit home run in World Series history, connecting off Ralph Branca in Game 3 against the Brooklyn Dodgers. 

🧩 TRIVIA: The Yankees still lost the game, 9–8, at Ebbets Field.

1953 — Brooklyn’s Carl Erskine, "Oisk" strikes out 14 New York Yankees in Game 3 of the World Series, a Fall Classic record at the time. 

🧩 TRIVIA: The mark lasted until Sandy Koufax fanned 15 Yankees in the 1963 Series opener.

1963 — Sandy Koufax, "The Left Arm of God" strikes out 15 New York Yankees as the Los Angeles Dodgers win Game 1 of the World Series, 5–2. 

🧩 TRIVIA: The 15 strikeouts stood as the World Series record for five years, until Bob Gibson’s 17 on this same date in 1968.

1965 — University of Florida players test a new drink, later named Gatorade, during a football game against LSU. 

🧩 TRIVIA: The formula was built to replace fluids and electrolytes lost in Florida heat, and it grew into a global sports-drink brand.

1968 — St. Louis Cardinals pitcher Bob "Gibby" Gibson,  strikes out 17 Detroit Tigers in a 4–0 shutout in Game 1 of the World Series. 

🧩 TRIVIA: Gibson beat 31-game winner Denny McLain and set a postseason strikeout record that still stands today.

1974 — Hank Aaron, "Hammerin' Hank" hits his 733rd home run, the last of his career as a member of the Atlanta Braves. 

🧩 TRIVIA: The homer also gave him 20 or more home runs in 20 straight seasons, a streak of his own.

1977 — Niki Lauda, "King Rat" finishes fourth in the United States Grand Prix East at Watkins Glen and clinches his second Formula 1 world title.  🏎️

🧩 TRIVIA: James Hunt, "the Shunt" won the race, a year after he had edged Lauda for the 1976 championship.

1980 — Larry Holmes, "The Easton Assassin" stops Muhammad Ali, "The Greatest" in the 11th round at Caesars Palace to keep the world heavyweight title. 

🧩 TRIVIA: Ali was 38 and trying to become champion for a fourth time; his trainer ended the fight.

1983 — The Green Bay Packers score 49 points in the first half and beat the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 55–14. 

🧩 TRIVIA: The 49 first-half points broke the NFL record of 45, which Green Bay itself had set against Cleveland in 1967.

1999 — Ray Bourque scores his 386th career goal and passes Paul Coffey for the most goals by a defenseman in NHL history. 

🧩 TRIVIA: The goal was Boston’s only score in a 3–1 season-opening loss to Carolina; Bourque finished his career with 410 goals.

2001 — Sammy Sosa, "Slammin' Sammy" homers for the Chicago Cubs and becomes the first player with three 60-home-run seasons. 

🧩 TRIVIA: The milestone came in a 5–4 loss to Cincinnati, off starter Lance Davis.

2004 — Jeff Kent, "The Big Kid" hits two home runs and passes Ryne Sandberg as the all-time home-run leader among second basemen. 

🧩 TRIVIA: Kent reached the mark with the Houston Astros in a 9–3 win over Colorado.

2016 — The United States regains the Ryder Cup, beating Europe 17–11 at Hazeltine National Golf Club. 

🧩 TRIVIA: Brooks Koepka, Brandt Snedeker, and Patrick Reed each won three matches for the American side.

● #PizzaDeliveryDay

September 30 is Pizza Delivery Day. One phone call, or a few taps on a smartphone, and a piping-hot pizza arrives at your door. This now-familiar service first came to Japan at the end of the Showa era.

The day was established by Domino's Pizza Japan, Inc., headquartered in #IwamotochoChiyoda, Tokyo, which operates the #DominosPizza delivery chain. On September 30, 1985, the first store, Domino's Pizza Ebisu, opened in #Ebisu, Tokyo, launching the very first pizza delivery service in Japan. That date became the observance itself. As a pioneer of the pizza delivery market, the company wanted to express gratitude for being part of the memories of families and friends, and the day was certified and registered by the Japan Anniversary Association in 2020. That year also marked the brand's 35th anniversary in Japan, celebrated with discount coupon giveaways.

Domino's Pizza traces its roots to #Michigan in the United States in 1960. Founder #ThomasMonaghan bought a small pizza shop for 500 dollars and came up with the idea of delivering pizza to students who lived far from the store and had no cars. In Japan, considering Tokyo's narrow and congested roads, a three-wheeled delivery scooter known as the #DominoGyro was developed. In 1986 the original Japanese menu item #TunaSpecial was launched, followed by the Japanese-style #CharcoalGrilledChickenTeriyaki in 1992, the smash hit #MayoJaga (mayonnaise and potato) in 1994, and the #QuattroPizza, which offers four flavors on one pie, in 1997, each one finding a place on Japanese dinner tables. In July 2019 the chain reached 600 stores, becoming number one in Japan among delivery pizza chains in both sales and store count.

Tonight, why not make dinner a time to share pizza with family or friends? While you are at it, try ordering one flavor you have never had alongside your usual favorite for a small adventure. The steam and cheers that rise when the box is opened become dinner-table memories that never fade. And after dinner, enjoy a sweet moment of caramel.

Earth Alliance
– From the Psi Corps pledge“"The Corps is mother, the Corps is father."
The Psi Corps was an Earth Alliance organization, ostensibly established to help human telepaths learn how to control and use their abilities for the betterment of themselves and Humanity at large.
Contents

1Culture of The Corps1.1Propaganda

2Resources2.1Psi Cops
2.2Bloodhound Units

2.3Directors of Psi Corps2.3.1Assistant Directors

3Terminology
4History4.1Early History
4.2Collaboration with the Shadows and the underground railroad
4.3Telepath War
4.4Aftermath

5References
Culture of The Corps
📷Psi Corps Badge
Psi Corps culture naturally grew out what had already been established by the Metasensory Regulation Authority, some of which came straight from The Kith. The phrase perhaps most synonymous with the Corps, "The Corps is Mother, The Corps is Father" came from MRA agent Desa Alexander, who along with her fellow Kith made a definite impression on Corps culture. She was frequent to remind her charges while training and tracking down blips that "The kith is mother. The kith is father." Another tradition that began with Alexander and one followed by many was the passing of family names within the Corps along the female line, rather than the male. Referred to as "Mitochondrial descent", the reason behind it was because the marker for the telepath gene was encoded within a teep's mitochondrial DNA. As such, Lyta Alexander could trace her linage back six generations to Desa herself, while Talia Winters inherited her name from former blip and resistance member Jenny Winters.[1] The practice was not totally pervasive however, and by the 2250s it had become something only really associated with the older families of the Corps.[2]
Children raised by the Corps were quickly and thoroughly indoctrinated. Raised mostly in Teeptown, they were kept in small groups or cadres where they were instilled with a sense of belonging and loyalty to a larger body, discouraging individual thinking and other solitary activities. Latents, children who had tested positive as teeps but had yet to manifest their psi abilities were kept in a separate dorm (sometimes called "the basement"), often shunned and rarely mixing with the others, however, once their talents manifested they would quickly be integrated into a proper cadre. Young teeps were taught that they were rare, special, and better than mundanes, and that two teeps should never be seen fighting in front of a normal.[2]
It is the position of the Psi Corps that telepathic humans who do not learn how to control their abilities are mostly unstable or become insane, therefore they need guidance. In addition to that, unregistered telepaths can do severe damage to society by using their abilities for criminal reasons.
Under Earth Alliance law, all human telepaths have to be registered with the Psi Corps. After that, they have three choices: Join the Psi Corps, lifetime imprisonment, or take drugs called sleepers to suppress their abilities. Most choose to work for Psi Corps, because one common side effect of the sleepers is severe depression, sometimes so severe that it often ends in the patient's suicide.[3] Unstable telepaths - such as schizophrenic ones - are locked away for "the good of everyone".[4]
Always an insular organization, Psi Corps would always try to deal with incidents (or "family matters") concerning telepaths internally and tried to avoid interference by mundanes. Believing that as long as normals were kept convinced "nothing goes wrong behind these walls", they would be left alone.[4]
I pledge my body, heart, soul and mind to the service of the Earth Alliance, and the people who dwell on her myriad spheres.
I promise to keep the laws, to keep the faith, to keep my eyes on the truth.
I pledge to serve my comrades, my cadre, and The Corps.
The Corps teaches, guides, and provides. The Corps is mother, the Corps is father.
We are the children of The Corps.
– The Psi Corps pledge.
Propaganda
To strengthen the dedication of telepaths to the Corps, there are a variety of slogans that shall remind the Telepaths, that Psi Corps is their family: -

"The Corps is mother, the Corps is father."
"The Psi Corps is your friend. Trust the Corps."
📷Psi Corps propaganda during an ISN transmission of 36 Hours.
"We’re everywhere. For your convenience."
"Protect the Family."

"Obey."

"Trust the Corps."

"Maternis, Paternis"

"United in thought, revered in memory."

Resources

Psi Corps facilities were spread across the Earth Alliance, from the Corps' headquarters in Earthdome to a secret intelligence center in Syria Planum on Mars.
The facilities at Earthdome featured hospitals, offices, and the Psi Corps Academy where young teeps and teeks were trained to make the best of their talents. Located nearby in Geneva was Teeptown, an enclosed community the size of a large village. Built out from the old MRA MetaSensory compound, this was where new members (mostly children) were indoctrinated into the culture and thinking of Psi Corps.
Unknown to many at the time, Psi Corps secretly maintained a series of motherships that remained in hyperspace. Ferrying Psi Cops back and forth on missions, the motherships only exited to normal space when maintenance and repairs were essential and could be done unobserved.
Psi Cops
📷Psi Cop training

Psi Cops is the collective name for officers of the Metasensory Police, or MetaPol and were the police enforcement arm of Psi Corps, usually dealing with cases relating to telepaths, mostly rogues and blips. All Psi Cops are P-12s,[5] the highest (natural) rating within the Psi Scale, but not every P-12 has the ability to become a Psi Cop, because it takes a certain amount of ruthlessness. Psi Cops receive a special training in blocking and scanning so that they are able to resist a deep-scan for at least an hour.[4]
Following the dissolution of the Psi Corps at the end of the Telepath War, the role of the Psi Cops was divided between the new Bureau of Telepath Integration and the new Metasensory Division of the Earth Alliance Bureau of Investigation.
Bloodhound Units

Bloodhound units are specially trained telepaths under the authority of the Psi Cops, used to hunt down fugitives through empathic tracking and scanning of witnesses, informants and suspects.
The origins of the Bloodhound Units go back to the days of the Metasensory Regulation Authority and a group of agents lead by Desa Alexander (also known as "Blood").[1]
Up until President Morgan Clark's increased dependence on the Psi Corps for civil intelligence gathering and black ops, the Bloodhounds were kept within the Corps, tracking blips and occasionally protecting their own.

One such incident occurred around 2253, when a serial killer murdered a string of commercial telepaths. With the "mundane" authorities seemingly uninterested in catching the perpetrator, the Psi Corps took matters into its own hands without such encumbrances as warrants, permission or due process. Illegally scanning anyone who might have a lead, the Bloodhounds left behind no traces save for lingering memory gaps, missing hours and headaches, eventually finding the killer. Reasoning that turning him over to the proper authorities would require an explanation as to how they found him, the Corps had him sent to an institution on Beta Colony instead, but not before they implanted visions and hallucinations in his mind so terrifying that he would spend the rest of his days and nights screaming at things that only he could see. To prevent him from clawing his own eyes out, he was kept in a straitjacket 24 hours a day.[6]
During the Earth Alliance Civil War, Bloodhound units were assigned to the Earthforce military divisions and bases occupying Mars. Anyone suspected of being a member of the resistance was subjected to a very deep scan. Given the nature of such invasive scans, they were prone to causing heart attacks, seizures, strokes, and even death.[6]
In 2262 the Bloodhound units were dispatched alongside Alfred Bester to hunt down Byron's dissident telepaths.[7][8]
Directors of Psi Corps
A lifelong position, the position of Director of Psi Corps was initially filled by normals who were appointed by the Earth Senate as stipulated in the Psi Corps' original charter. Eventually the position was given over to telepaths.
People who have held the position
Lee Crawford (April 12 - May 19 2161)

Kevin Vacit (2161 - 2195)

Johnston (2195 - 2256)

Assistant Directors
At any one time, the Psi Corps has had four Assistant Directors, with at least one permanently stationed on Mars.[2]
People who have held the position
Menendez (Earth, Circa 2253)

Kaufman (Mars, Circa 2253)

Drake (Earth, Circa 2262)

Terminology
Basement: Informal name given to the dormitory for latent children. These children are kept separate from other telepaths until their abilities manifest, at which point they are integrated into an appropriate Cadre.[2]

Black Omega: Elite Starfury unit attached to Psi Corps.[9]

Blip: a general term used by security officers for fugitives from the law, though it has also become synonymous with rogue telepaths.[9][10] "Type A" Blips are considered to be merely misguided and open to re-education. "Type C" Blips are those who are considered sociopaths or "born criminals", who enjoy abusing their abilities and are much more difficult to re-educate.[2]

Bloop: Referring to the involuntary broadcasting of stray thoughts, either through weak blocks, poor discipline and/or loss of control through panic and emotional distress. Very young or untrained teeps, as well as teeks of any age are particularly notorious for blooping.[2]

Block: Telepathic guard against active scanning or passive sensing. Blocks usually take the form of repeating songs, nursery rhymes, or mathematical calculations.[11][12] With training, mundanes can also use these techniques to block an active scan, although the mundane's ability to resist depends on how strong the telepath is.[13] Blocks can be broken by a sufficiently strong and/ or well trained teep, however doing so forcefully can lead to the subject suffering strokes, aneurysms or cerebral hemorrhaging.[11]
This can also refer to subconscious conditioning that restrains a subject at the point of action.[2][8]

Boot: Psi Corps security officers. Not full Psi Cops, they usually operated in support roles such as Bloodhound units.[2]

Bloodhound: Psi Corps tracking units, usually operating under the direction of a full Psi Cop.[2]
Busybody: Slang term for a commercial telepath.[2]
Cadre: Training groups composed of young telepaths, organized into boarding houses according to age group.[2]

Cadre Prime: A cadre of telepaths whose abilities manifested either at birth or before the onset of puberty. Housed separately from the other cadres, they account for less than 5% of all telepaths, and as such they are considered exceptionally rare and special. Other Cadres include Cadre Secundus and Cadre Tertius.[2]
Casting: (See "Mindcast")
Cops 'n' Blips: An approved game played by children in the Psi Corps during "constructive playtime". Generally it involves one or two children ("the blips") who are tasked with getting to a prearranged location without being caught, while the others (the "cops") attempt to track and capture them.[2]
Deathbed Scan: Performed when a telepath combs a dying person's mind for vital information up until the very moment of death. Such scans are known to be harmful to the telepath's mental health, with some believing that one loses a piece of one's soul by being in contact with the soon-to-decease person as they cross the threshold. Almost no telepath who has done such a scan willingly does one a second time, since subsequent attempts are thought to be very damaging to the psyche.[12] Psi Cop Alfred Bester repeatedly volunteered for such duty, once even following a subject's mind into the void. During that scan Bester very nearly died himself, and would have if not for the resuscitation efforts of hospital staff attending the dying subject. Some in the Corps say that Bester is the way he is because the better part of his soul is missing.[12]
Fugue: Telepathic attack. A favorite trick of blips, a fugue forces the target's mind to suddenly repeat its last thought over and over, effectively freezing the person's mind in the moment. The effect is short lived, but if timed right it can be enough to give the attacker an edge.[1] For a telepath, a fugue state is akin to a psi seizure or stroke, and can sometimes be brought on by extremely severe emotional distress or shock.[2]
Grabber, The: A children's nickname for William Karges and the statue that bore his likeness in Teeptown's alpha quad. Destroyed during the Telepath War, what was left was eventually removed and replaced by a statue of Matthew and Fiona Dexter with their lost baby Stephen in 2281.[14]

Grins: Term used by Psi Corps children for the faceless monitors within Psi Corps Cadre Prime youth training programs. Noted for their grey robes, almost mechanical voices, impersonal nature, and their blank featureless masks that display only very basic emotional symbols. Dealing out both punishments and rewards, they are more often than not a source of apprehension and mystery for most teep children. At age 12, the children are shown the true identities of the Grins, who are revealed to be their teachers and caregivers during a ceremony in which they receive their first pair of gloves.[2]
Glyph: Projection of a telepathic image. Can be used as a means of deception (making a subject think they saw something they didn't) or to accentuate communication through illustration.[2]
John Trakker, Psi Cop: Fictional character that features in a weekly vid series produced by the Psi Corps. A Psi Cop that works with his partner Heng, every week they work to capture "evil" and "stupid" rogue telepaths and send them off to be re-educated by the Corps. Also featured on a merchandising line based on the show.[2]
Latent: Referring to a telepath who has scored positive on the screening test, but whose ability has not yet manifested. Also called "late bloomers".[2][11][15]
Later: Referring to a telepath whose ability manifested after or during puberty.[2]
Mindblast: A sudden and powerful brute-force telepathic attack, a mindblast leaves its target in a telepathic fugue. Partial amnesia is also a common side effect of a mindblast.[2]
Mindburst: A sudden and debilitating burst of background "noise" from other minds, most commonly suffered by laters as their psi ability first manifests itself. The mindburst's intensity is directly proportional to the teep's psi rating. For example, to a P10 the experience is akin to a deaf person suddenly hearing a rocket engine right by their heads. The sudden shock can be severe enough as to render a teep unconscious.[16]
Mindcast: Direct telepathic communication.[2]
Mind shredder: Term applied to an individual trained in attack probes who has an exceptional knack for disrupting the abilities of other telepaths.[4]
Mindquake: A localized kinetic agitation, usually the result of an unstable teek who is unable to control their ability.[5]
Monitors: (See "Grins")
Mundane: non-telepath, meaning literally "normal". Often pejorative.[9]
P'see: Term used for a telepathic perception that manifests and is interpreted by a teep's brain as visual information, a sort of telepathic sight. Similar terms include "p'squint" and "p'hear".[2]
Psi Cop: Psi Corps police officers.
Rogue: (See "Blip")
Scan: An active telepathic probe. Surface scans, while difficult for even a trained P5 to detect, can only reveal what a person happens to be thinking from moment to moment and is routinely used in business negotiations to detect falsehoods, omission and obfuscation. A deep scan, while often uncomfortable, can uncover deeper thoughts and memories. Under certain conditions deep and extended scans can cause seizures, heart attacks, strokes, permanent brain damage, or if the subject is particularly resistant, death. Sustaining and blocking extended scans can also affect the telepath running the scan - the best human telepaths can only sustain a deep scan for up to 40–45 minutes, at which time they burst arteries, have strokes, or black out.[2][4][5][17]
Teep: Referring to any telepath.[15]
Teeptown: Closed community for telepaths in Geneva, originally built up by the MRA and later Psi Corps from the old "metasensory compound".[1][2]
Teek: Referring to any telekinetic. Noted for their tendency to "bloop".[15]
History
📷Psi Corps Headquarters
Early History
The beginnings of The Corps date back to 2117 and the formation of the Metasensory Regulation Authority (itself an outgrowth of the 2115 Senate Committee on Technology and Privacy and the subsequent Committee on Metasensory Regulation.) In 2156, following first contact with the Centauri Republic and the revelation that the Centauri and many other alien races possessed telepaths, it became apparent that Earth would need a more permanent and comprehensive solution than the MRA was able to provide. What finally tipped the balance of public opinion was the self-sacrifice of Earthforce Security Commander William Karges in thwarting of an assassination attempt on EA President Elizabeth Robinson in October of 2160. Karges had been an unregistered telepath and had used his ability to sense the thoughts of the bombers before they could detonate the President's motorcade. With this swing in public opinion concerning telepaths (which had until this point had been at its lowest since the pogroms of 2115), on April 12 2161, President Robinson was finally able to realize what Senator Lee Crawford had been working toward for decades and institute universal registration for Earth Alliance telepaths and an independently chartered MRA, dubbed "Psi Corps." Though the Karges incident is often credited by Psi Corps propaganda as the deciding factor, more cynical students of history have compared it to George Washington chopping down a cherry tree.[1][2][18] Robinson immediately offered Crawford the position of Director of the Psi Corps, though his tenure was short-lived, as on May 19, 2161, Crawford was assassinated while on his way to a meeting with Earth's first Centauri ambassador. Kevin Vacit, Crawford's assistant of nearly 30 years became the new Director.
While its public image was always that of a "friendly" service to society (though the facade was at times rather thin), under Vacit's direction, Psi Corps was fashioned into a keenly balanced machine, dedicated to honing and cultivating telepaths for the inevitable day when co-existence with mundanes would become a matter of survival. So adept was he at setting the Corps on its course that it could continue without him and without even knowing its true purpose.[1]
Collaboration with the Shadows and the underground railroad
Doctor Stephen Franklin participated in an underground railroad to help rogue telepaths escape from the Corps. Eventually, some of the telepaths who escaped provided assistance during the closing days of the Second Shadow war, while the highest levels of the Corps allied itself with the Shadows, providing them with captured rogue telepaths to operate on and surgically alter. Via Morden, the Shadows took an active role in the assassination of Luis Santiago, allowing some of their technology to be used by Earthforce.
After the Shadows and Vorlons left the galaxy with the other First Ones and Clark's defeat following the end of the Earth Alliance Civil War, a group of rogue telepaths led by Byron formed a small colony on Babylon 5, granted sanctuary by ISA President John Sheridan. The situation later ended in violence when the Psi Cops attempted to take the rogue telepaths back to Earth.
Telepath War
After the colony on Babylon 5 was forced to leave following the death of its leader, Byron, Lyta Alexander began a crusade against the Psi Corps. Her actions led to a conflict in which both rogue telepaths and mundanes fought against the Psi Corps. This conflict would later become known as the Telepath War.
Having lost the power it held during the Clark administration, the Psi Corps attempted to take over Earth's government, but eventually was defeated by the Earth Alliance, aided by the Interstellar Alliance and the rogue telepaths.
Aftermath
Following the end of the Telepath War, Psi Corps was formally dissolved, and the Earth Alliance began to take steps to re-integrate its telepaths into mainstream society. Freeing them from many of the past rules and restrictions, teeps were now allowed a much wider range of options as to what they chose to do with their lives, such as serving in Earthforce and working in the private sector. Many private schools were set up to educate telepaths around this time, though their success rate was somewhat mixed.
After the dissolution of Psi Corps, the Psionic Monitoring Commission was created, dedicated to hunting down those members of the Corps who had committed war crimes such as Alfred Bester. Eventually captured and put on trial for his past atrocities, Bester was sentenced to spend the rest of his life in prison, his abilities taken away by the very sleepers that he once administered to countless blips.
Some Psi Corps members, like John Matheson, joined later Earthforce.

text:
Jaleel McLaughlin ran 28 yards into the end zone tonight as the Cleveland Browns beat the Pittsburgh Steelers 27-24.

His mother Tonya lost her factory job when he was 12. The Ford Focus is where they ended up.

His grandmother had already died of a heart attack while the family was living in her house.

They stayed in motels before that. They stayed with relatives. Tonya was raising him and his siblings by herself, and then she had to take work in Arkansas and was apart from her sons for two years. They got back together right as he started high school.

He was good. At Forest Hills High School in Marshville, North Carolina he won a state title in basketball, two more in track, and averaged 8.4 yards a carry as a senior running back.

Almost nobody offered him a scholarship. He is 5 foot 7. The few schools that called mostly wanted to move him to defensive back.

Notre Dame College took him. Division II. South Euclid, Ohio, ten miles east of Cleveland.

He ran for 302 yards in his first college game. A Division II record.

Then 2,421 yards as a freshman. Then 2,316 yards and 33 touchdowns as a sophomore. He transferred to Youngstown State and kept going.

He finished with 8,166 yards and 79 touchdowns.

Read that again. Nobody in the history of college football, in any division, has ever run for more yards than Jaleel McLaughlin.

He went undrafted in 2023.

The Denver Broncos signed him off the street. He played all 17 games as a rookie.

Here is the part that gets me.

Notre Dame College, where he set those records, closed its doors for good on May 2, 2024. The school does not exist anymore. There is no team to go back to.

On September 1 of this year the Cleveland Browns put him on their practice squad. On September 15 they moved him up to the active roster after Dylan Sampson got hurt.

Tonight, ten miles from a campus that is gone, in a three point game against the team Cleveland hates most, he took it 28 yards and scored.

"Have a goal, have a dream," he said when he broke the record. "Don't let nobody tell you what you can be, no matter the circumstance, no matter how small, no matter where you come from."

Be honest about where he stands. He is a backup. He went from Denver to a practice squad to a roster spot that only opened because somebody else got injured. Next September is not promised to him either.

But he has already done the hardest thing he will ever do, and it had nothing to do with football.

A kid who slept in a Ford Focus is playing on Thursday night in prime time.
